cells.tense: Present — here, holding what you hold and setting down what you don't, at the same pace.
cells.verb: moving steadily without having to push
cells.place: in the act of letting go of what's finished
cells.ask: Picture one thing you'd actually want in the space you've just cleared — not a replacement, a wish — and let yourself want it for a day.
cells.core:
You're letting go at a walking pace. Nothing dramatic about it — something stops serving and your hands open, and you keep moving. The things you set down don't trail behind you, and the setting down doesn't cost you your stride. That's not detachment; it's that your wanting and your doing are pointed the same way, so the clearing is just part of the going.

There's room now. If you want it, that room can be for imagining — not what you'd fill it with to feel safe, but what you'd want there because you've fully lived what came before and can see past it.
cells.sheetLine: You let go at a walking pace, and the going doesn't stop.

cells.tense: Future — you're already living in the lighter version of yourself, the one who has let it all go, and you're hurrying toward her.
cells.verb: pushing the momentum harder than the moment asks
cells.place: in the act of letting go of what's finished
cells.ask: Before the next thing goes, put the whole picture on one page — what you've let go, what you're still holding, and what you're not sure about yet — and sit with the full list before you cross anything off.
cells.core:
You're letting go ahead of your own feeling. There's a version of you somewhere up the road who's shed everything that weighed on her, and you're trying to get there by dropping things faster — before you've felt what they were, before you've checked whether they're actually finished. Momentum that used to feel like your own rhythm has turned into a march, and the clearing has started to look like clearing out.

The steadiness comes back when direction comes from what you actually feel, not from what you've decided to be rid of. That takes a wider view than one thing at a time.
cells.sheetLine: You're letting go faster than you can feel what's leaving.

cells.tense: Past — you're still standing at a door you decided to walk through some time ago.
cells.verb: the steady forward motion that won't start
cells.place: in the act of letting go of what's finished
cells.ask: Name one thing you let go of before — something that ended — and write down what it actually gave you afterward, what you would have missed by holding on. Count the yield, not the loss.
cells.core:
You know what no longer serves. You've known a while. And the part of you that usually moves — the part that walks forward without having to be dragged — isn't moving here. The grip stays closed, the rhythm you trust in everything else has stalled at this one threshold, and the door is behind you even though you haven't gone through it.

Forcing your hands open won't do it. What tends to work is remembering what past endings grew: when you've looked at what a release gave you, trusting the next one gets easier, and the motion comes back on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's finished and you can't get yourself to move.

cells.tense: Present, disowned — you're already doing this, and you keep saying it's happening to you.
cells.verb: moving steadily on your own power
cells.place: in the act of letting go of what's finished
cells.ask: Pick one thing that has 'just fallen away' and set it down on purpose this time — choose the day, say it's your choice, and keep choosing, one small deliberate release at a time.
cells.core:
Things have been leaving your life at a steady pace — habits, obligations, people, old versions of plans. You describe it as drift. 'It just stopped mattering.' 'That faded out.' But look at how evenly it's happening, and how little it costs you each time: that's not weather. That's you, setting things down with a rhythm that's yours, and declining to sign the work.

When the steering is claimed, direction can come from what you feel instead of what seems to happen. The way there is simpler than it sounds — the plain, repeated act of doing it on purpose.
cells.sheetLine: You've been letting go on purpose. You call it things falling away.
